decks.title: Print Culture and the Modern World — Part 1: From Woodblocks to the Reading Mania
goals: Trace print from woodblock printing in China and Japan to Gutenberg's press
Explain how print created a reading public and fed religious debate and the French Revolution
Describe how children, women and workers became new readers in the nineteenth century
Answer a source-based question and a 5-mark question the way examiners mark them

slides.heading: Print Culture and the Modern World
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how a technology born in East Asia changed what people read, believed and argued about, from China in the sixth century to Europe in the nineteenth.

nodes.label: From AD 594: woodblock books in China

visual.alt: Timeline of Part 1: woodblock books in China from AD 594, the Diamond Sutra in Japan in AD 868, Marco Polo's return in 1295, Gutenberg's press by 1448, Luther's theses in 1517, and the reading mania and mass printing of the nineteenth century
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Namaste! Hold up any book, newspaper or notice near you. It is so ordinary that we forget printing once seemed like magic, and sometimes like danger. In this chapter we follow print from Chinese woodblocks to the steam-powered presses of the eighteen hundreds. Watch for one big question: when ideas can be copied cheaply and quickly, who gains power, and who tries to stop them?

slides.heading: Print begins in East Asia

rows: Pages carved in wood, inked, and pressed onto paper by hand; "accordion" books, printed on one side, folded and stitched
The imperial state printed textbooks for the civil service examinations
Merchants, leisure readers and rich women read fiction, poetry and plays; some women published
Western mechanical presses; Shanghai emerges as the new centre of printing

visual.alt: Table of print in China: woodblock books from AD 594 printed on one side and folded; state printing for the civil service examinations; seventeenth-century leisure reading by merchants and women; and late nineteenth-century Western presses with Shanghai as the hub

slides.narration: The story starts in China. From the late sixth century, printers carved a page into a block of wood, inked it, and rubbed paper over it. The paper was so thin that only one side could be printed, so pages were folded like an accordion and stitched. For centuries the biggest printer was the state, producing textbooks for the civil service examinations. Later, merchants and women became eager readers too.

slides.heading: Print in Japan
slides.body_md: Buddhist missionaries from China brought **hand-printing** to Japan around **AD 768–770**.

rows: Oldest Japanese printed book: the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, six sheets of text with woodcut pictures
Poets and prose writers published regularly; books were cheap and plentiful
Kitagawa Utamaro and the art of ukiyo, "pictures of the floating world", showing city life

visual.alt: Table of print in Japan: the Diamond Sutra of AD 868 with six sheets and woodcuts; regular publishing in medieval Japan; and in late eighteenth-century Edo, Utamaro and the ukiyo art of everyday city life

slides.narration: From China, printing travelled to Japan with Buddhist missionaries in the eight hundreds. The oldest Japanese printed book, from eight sixty-eight, is the Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist text with pictures cut in wood. By the seventeen hundreds, the city of Edo, which we now call Tokyo, was full of bookshops and libraries. Artists like Utamaro made prints of everyday city life, called ukiyo.

slides.heading: Quick check: Japan
slides.narration: Who carried printing to Japan, and roughly when? Decide before you answer.

slides.heading: From scribes to a printing press

nodes.label: 1295: Marco Polo brings knowledge of woodblock printing from China to Italy
Woodblocks spread; used for textiles, playing cards and religious pictures
Scribes cannot keep up with demand; manuscripts costly and fragile
Gutenberg adapts the olive press and casts metal type
By 1448: system perfected; the Bible printed

visual.alt: Flow: Marco Polo brought knowledge of woodblock printing to Italy in 1295; woodblocks spread for textiles, cards and religious pictures; scribes could not meet demand; Gutenberg adapted the olive press and cast metal type; by 1448 the system was perfected and the Bible printed

slides.narration: Europe learnt of woodblock printing when Marco Polo came home from China in twelve ninety-five. Woodblocks spread, but books were still mostly copied by hand, slowly and at great cost. Johann Gutenberg, a goldsmith who had grown up around wine and olive presses, put two ideas together: a screw press, and movable letters cast in metal. By fourteen forty-eight his system worked. His first great book was the Bible.

slides.heading: The print revolution
slides.body_md: Between **1450 and 1550**, printing presses were set up in most countries of Europe.

x.label: Period (1 = second half of the 1400s, 2 = the 1500s)

visual.alt: Bar chart: about 20 million copies of books were printed in Europe in the second half of the fifteenth century, and about 200 million in the sixteenth century
visual.caption: Bar 1: second half of the 1400s, about 20 million copies. Bar 2: the 1500s, about 200 million copies.

slides.narration: Here is the scale of the change. In the second half of the fourteen hundreds, European presses turned out about twenty million copies of books. In the next century, the figure rose to about two hundred million, ten times as many. Books became cheaper, quicker to make, and far more common. Historians call this the print revolution: not just a new machine, but a new relationship between people and knowledge.

slides.heading: From listening to reading
columns:
**Before print**

- Knowledge passed on by word of mouth
- Ordinary people heard sacred texts read out
- Ballads and folk tales were sung and told

**After print**

- Books reached a wider reading public
- But literacy stayed low for long
- So printed ballads and tales were read aloud in villages and taverns

visual.alt: Table comparing a world of listeners, where knowledge was spoken and sung and controlled by priests and scholars, with a world of readers, where knowledge was printed and read and many authors and printers shaped it

slides.narration: Before print, most people heard knowledge rather than read it. A priest read the scriptures; a singer sang the ballads. Print created a reading public. But do not overstate it. Many people still could not read, so printers sold ballads and folk tales that were read aloud at village gatherings. Spoken and printed culture blended. This mixing is a useful point in long answers.

slides.heading: Print, faith and fear

nodes.label: 1517: Luther's Ninety Five Theses criticise Church practices
Printed copies spread fast; German New Testament sells out
Readers like Menocchio form their own beliefs
Church response: Inquisition; Index of Prohibited Books from 1558

visual.alt: Flow: Luther's Ninety Five Theses of 1517 spread rapidly in print, his New Testament sold out, the Reformation followed, readers like Menocchio formed their own beliefs, and the Church responded with the Inquisition and the Index of Prohibited Books from 1558

slides.narration: In fifteen seventeen, Martin Luther wrote ninety-five arguments against practices of the Roman Catholic Church. Printers copied them by the thousand, and his German New Testament sold out within weeks. Print helped the Reformation spread. It also let ordinary readers think for themselves. A miller called Menocchio read books and formed his own ideas of God. The Church tried him and executed him, and began keeping a list of forbidden books.

slides.heading: Quick check: Luther and print
slides.body_md: Decide whether the assertion and the reason are true, and whether the reason explains the assertion.
slides.narration: Is the assertion true? Is the reason true? Does print explain the speed?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a source-based question, step by step
slides.body_md: Source (written by SOYL): *An imagined letter from a Venetian printer, 1560, says a priest has brought him a list of books he may no longer sell, and that a customer was questioned for owning a forbidden book.*
bullets: Step 1 — Read the questions first.
Step 2 — (a) "Name the list" (1 mark): the Index of Prohibited Books.
Step 3 — (b) "Who issued it?" (1 mark): the Roman Catholic Church.
Step 4 — (c) "Why did the Church fear print?" (2 marks): source point (customers owning forbidden books) + knowledge point (readers such as Menocchio formed views the Church called heresy).
Step 5 — Two clear points, about 40 words.

rows: 1 for the source point + 1 for linking to wider knowledge

visual.alt: Table: parts a and b earn one mark each for precise facts; part c earns two marks, one for the source point and one for wider knowledge

slides.narration: Here is the method again. Read the questions first. One-mark parts need one precise answer: the Index of Prohibited Books, issued by the Roman Catholic Church. The two-mark part asks why. Take one point from the source, that ordinary people owned forbidden books, and add one from your knowledge, such as the case of Menocchio. Keep it to about forty words.

slides.heading: The reading mania

rows: Up to 60–80 per cent in some areas by 1800
Penny chapbooks in England; Biliotheque Bleue in France
Newspapers and journals mixing news and entertainment
Isaac Newton; Thomas Paine, Voltaire, Rousseau

visual.alt: Table of the reading mania: literacy rising to 60 to 80 per cent in some areas by 1800; pedlars selling penny chapbooks and the Biliotheque Bleue; periodicals mixing news and entertainment; and the ideas of Newton, Paine, Voltaire and Rousseau reaching ordinary readers

slides.narration: In the seventeen and eighteen hundreds, Europe went book-crazy. Churches opened village schools, and in some areas most adults could read by eighteen hundred. Pedlars walked from village to village with cheap little books: almanacs, ballads, folk tales. In England these were penny chapbooks; in France, books with cheap blue covers. Newspapers and journals spread, and the ideas of scientists and philosophers reached ordinary readers.

slides.heading: Print and the French Revolution

nodes.label: Enlightenment ideas spread: Voltaire, Rousseau attack tradition and despotism
A new habit of public argument: every value open to question
1780s: writing and cartoons mock royalty and their morals
Caution: readers also read royal and Church writing and made up their own minds

visual.alt: Flow: three arguments, the spread of Enlightenment ideas, a culture of debate, and satire of the royal family, lead people to question authority, with the caution that readers also read royal and Church writing and made up their own minds

slides.narration: Did books cause the French Revolution? Historians offer three arguments. Print spread the ideas of thinkers like Voltaire and Rousseau. It created a culture of argument in which every tradition could be questioned. And by the seventeen eighties, pamphlets and cartoons mocked the royal family. But be careful. People also read royal and Church writing, and judged for themselves. Print made new thinking possible; it did not force it.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a 5-mark "evaluate" answer
slides.body_md: Question: *"Print created the French Revolution." How far do you agree?* (about 120 words)
bullets: Step 1 — State a position in one line: print helped create the conditions, but did not cause the Revolution alone.
Step 2 — Give three supporting points: Enlightenment ideas, a culture of debate, satire of royalty.
Step 3 — Give one counter-point: readers also read royal and Church writing and interpreted ideas in their own way.
Step 4 — End with a judgement that weighs both sides.

visual.alt: Table of five marks for an evaluate answer: a position, Enlightenment ideas, debate and satire, a counter-point that readers were not passive, and a judgement

slides.narration: Evaluate questions want a judgement, not just a list. Start by taking a clear position: print helped create the conditions, but did not cause the Revolution alone. Back it with evidence, then show the other side: readers were not sponges; they read royal writing too and made up their own minds. Finish with a sentence that weighs both. That structure earns the top marks.

slides.heading: New readers in the nineteenth century

rows: School textbooks; a children's press (France, 1857); folk tales edited for the young
The Grimm brothers' tales (1812), with "unsuitable" material removed
Penny magazines, manuals on conduct and housekeeping, novels
Novelists Jane Austen, the Brontë sisters, George Eliot
Lending libraries; workers' own tracts and autobiographies
Shorter working hours gave time to read and write

visual.alt: Table of new readers: children with textbooks, a children's press in France in 1857 and edited Grimm tales; women with magazines, manuals and novels by Austen, the Brontës and Eliot; workers with lending libraries and their own tracts and autobiographies

slides.narration: The eighteen hundreds discovered new kinds of readers. Children got textbooks when primary schooling became compulsory, and even a press of their own in France. The Grimm brothers collected peasant folk tales, but cut what seemed unfit for children. Women read magazines and novels, and women novelists like Jane Austen and the Brontë sisters wrote heroines with minds of their own. Workers used lending libraries and wrote their own life stories.

slides.heading: Quick check: cheap books
slides.narration: Think of the English pedlars and the price of what they sold.

slides.heading: Faster presses, new kinds of books

nodes.label: Mid-1800s: Hoe's power-driven cylindrical press, about 8,000 sheets an hour
Late 1800s: offset press, up to six colours at once
Early 1900s: electric presses, automatic paper reels

visual.alt: Flow of printing technology: metal presses in the late eighteenth century; Hoe's cylindrical press printing about 8,000 sheets an hour in the mid nineteenth; offset presses printing up to six colours in the late nineteenth; electric presses in the early twentieth; and new forms such as serialised novels, shilling series and paperbacks

slides.narration: Machines kept getting faster. In the mid eighteen hundreds, Richard Hoe of New York built a power-driven cylindrical press that could print about eight thousand sheets an hour, perfect for newspapers. Later, offset presses printed in up to six colours, and electric presses sped things further. Publishers invented new ways to sell: novels in weekly instalments, cheap shilling series, and, during the Depression of the nineteen thirties, paperbacks.

slides.heading: Quick check: in order
slides.body_md: Arrange these milestones from earliest to latest.
slides.narration: Write a date beside each milestone, then order them.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: China (woodblocks from AD 594; state textbooks; Shanghai later); Japan (Diamond Sutra, AD 868; ukiyo)
Marco Polo 1295; Gutenberg by 1448; presses across Europe 1450–1550
Cheaper books; a reading public; oral and print culture mix
Luther 1517; Menocchio; Index of Prohibited Books 1558
Enlightenment ideas, debate, satire of royalty, with limits
Children, women, workers as readers; faster presses; new forms

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: print in East Asia, the arrival of print in Europe, the print revolution, religion and print, the French Revolution, and nineteenth-century readers and technology

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Printing began with Chinese woodblocks and spread to Japan. Europe learnt of it through Marco Polo, and Gutenberg's press made books cheap and plentiful. A reading public emerged, but spoken culture lived on. Print helped Luther and worried the Church. It helped people question kings before the French Revolution. And in the eighteen hundreds, children, women and workers became readers, served by ever-faster presses.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Woodblock (China, Japan) vs movable metal type (Gutenberg): do not mix them up.
On print and the French Revolution, give the three arguments and one caution.
Menocchio was a miller and a reader, not a printer.
Chapbooks are English; the Biliotheque Bleue is French.
In 5-mark answers, use five distinct points with key terms.
slides.narration: Before your test, check these traps. Woodblocks belong to China and Japan; movable metal type belongs to Gutenberg. For the French Revolution, give all three arguments and then a caution, because evaluation questions reward balance. Menocchio was a reader who formed his own beliefs, not a printer. And remember which cheap books belong to which country: chapbooks in England, blue-covered books in France.

decks.title: Print Culture and the Modern World — Part 2: India and the World of Print
goals: Explain how print spread in India and how it shaped religious reform debates
Describe new forms of publication and visual culture
Explain how women, poor people and workers became readers and writers
Analyse print and censorship under colonial rule

slides.heading: India and the world of print
slides.body_md: Part 2 — from palm-leaf manuscripts to newspapers that worried an empire.

visual.alt: Timeline of Part 2: the first press in Goa in the mid sixteenth century, the first Tamil book at Cochin in 1579, Hickey's Bengal Gazette in 1780, Sambad Kaumudi in 1821, the Vernacular Press Act in 1878 and Tilak's imprisonment in 1908
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to Part 2. India had a rich tradition of handwritten books long before the printing press arrived. When print came, first with missionaries and then with traders and reformers, it changed how Indians argued about religion, how women and workers found a voice, and how people in distant regions began to feel connected. It also made the colonial government nervous. Let us see why.

slides.heading: Before print: the manuscript tradition

rows: Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian and many vernaculars
Palm leaves or handmade paper; often illustrated; bound between wooden covers or sewn
Costly, fragile, hard to read because of varied scripts; little everyday use
Pupils learnt to write from dictation; pupils could write well yet had never handled a book

visual.alt: Table of the manuscript tradition: written in Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian and vernaculars on palm leaves or handmade paper, often illustrated; costly, fragile and hard to read; and in Bengal village schools pupils learnt to write from dictation

slides.narration: India's manuscripts were beautiful: written on palm leaves or handmade paper, in Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian and many regional languages, often with painted illustrations. But they were expensive, fragile, and written in scripts that were not easy to read, so few people used them every day. In Bengal's village schools, teachers recited passages from memory and pupils wrote them down. Many could write well yet had never held a book of their own.

slides.heading: Print arrives in India

rows: First press, brought by Portuguese missionaries; Jesuits print in Konkani
First Tamil book, printed by Catholic priests
James Augustus Hickey's weekly Bengal Gazette
Gangadhar Bhattacharya, close to Rammohun Roy, brings out a weekly Bengal Gazette, the first Indian-run newspaper

visual.alt: Table of early print in India: the first press in Goa in the mid sixteenth century, the first Tamil book at Cochin in 1579, the first Malayalam book in 1713, Hickey's Bengal Gazette in Calcutta in 1780, and the first Indian-run weekly by Gangadhar Bhattacharya in 1816

slides.narration: The first press came to Goa with Portuguese missionaries in the fifteen hundreds. Jesuit priests learnt Konkani and printed religious tracts. The first Tamil book was printed at Cochin in fifteen seventy-nine. English newspapers came later. In seventeen eighty, James Augustus Hickey began the Bengal Gazette in Calcutta, and by eighteen sixteen Indians, like Gangadhar Bhattacharya, a friend of Rammohun Roy, were publishing their own papers.

slides.heading: Quick check: the first press
slides.narration: Who brought the first press, and where did they live and work?

slides.heading: Hickey and the Governor-General
slides.body_md: Hickey's weekly proudly claimed to be **independent of colonial influence**.

nodes.label: Bengal Gazette prints advertisements and gossip about senior Company officials
An early lesson: the state wants to control what is printed

visual.alt: Flow: the Bengal Gazette printed advertisements and gossip about senior Company officials; Warren Hastings persecuted Hickey and encouraged approved newspapers, an early sign of the state wanting to control print

slides.narration: Hickey's paper printed advertisements, including some for the sale of slaves, and plenty of gossip about senior officials of the East India Company. Governor-General Warren Hastings did not enjoy reading about himself. He persecuted Hickey and encouraged newspapers that carried the official line. Notice the pattern, because it repeats through this chapter: whenever print gave people a voice, those in power tried to control it.

slides.heading: Print and religious debate

rows: Sambad Kaumudi (Rammohun Roy, 1821) vs Samachar Chandrika
Cheap lithographed translations of scripture; religious papers; fatwas
Ramcharitmanas printed 1810; Naval Kishore Press, Lucknow; Shri Venkateshwar Press, Bombay
Jam-i-Jahan Nama and Shamsul Akhbar (1822); Bombay Samachar (1822)

visual.alt: Table of print and religion: reformers and orthodox Hindus with Sambad Kaumudi and Samachar Chandrika; the ulama with lithographed translations and Deoband's fatwas; devotional texts such as the Ramcharitmanas from 1810 and the Naval Kishore and Shri Venkateshwar presses; and Persian and Gujarati newspapers of 1822

slides.narration: In the early eighteen hundreds, Indians argued fiercely about religion and custom, and print became the arena. Rammohun Roy argued for reform in Sambad Kaumudi, and orthodox Hindus answered in the Samachar Chandrika. Muslim scholars, worried about colonial rule, printed translations of scripture and, at Deoband, a flood of fatwas on daily life. Cheap editions of texts like the Ramcharitmanas could be read anywhere, and read aloud to those who could not read.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a source-based question, step by step
slides.body_md: Source (written by SOYL): *An imagined letter from a schoolteacher in Lucknow, 1885, describes villagers gathering every evening to hear a cheap printed copy of the Ramcharitmanas read aloud, and a neighbour who orders a Persian newspaper from Calcutta.*
bullets: Step 1 — Read the questions first.
Step 2 — (a) "Name a Lucknow press that printed religious texts" (1 mark): the Naval Kishore Press.
Step 3 — (b) "How did non-readers enjoy the book?" (1 mark): it was read aloud to them, from the source.

Step 4 — (c) "How did print connect people across India?" (2 marks): source point (a paper from Calcutta read in Lucknow) + knowledge point (common texts and news helped create pan-Indian identities).

visual.alt: Table: part a tests recall for one mark, part b finding information in the source for one mark, and part c explaining with the source and wider knowledge for two marks

slides.narration: Look at how the marks build up. Part a is a fact you must know: the Naval Kishore Press in Lucknow. Part b is in the source: the book was read aloud. Part c asks you to connect. Use the newspaper from Calcutta as your source point, and add your own knowledge that shared texts and news helped people far apart feel part of one community.

slides.heading: New forms and new pictures

rows: A European form that took on Indian styles and themes
New ways to write about social and political life
Raja Ravi Varma's images for mass circulation; cheap prints and calendars sold in bazaars
Comment on society and politics: some mocked Westernised Indians, some feared change, some attacked imperial rule, some lampooned nationalists

visual.alt: Table of new forms: the novel taking Indian forms; lyrics, short stories and essays; pictures for mass circulation by Raja Ravi Varma and cheap calendars; and by the 1870s cartoons commenting on society and politics from many sides

slides.narration: Print brought new ways of writing and seeing. The novel, a European form, became thoroughly Indian in its themes and style. Writers tried lyrics, short stories and essays. Artists like Raja Ravi Varma produced images for mass circulation, and cheap prints and calendars hung in ordinary homes. By the eighteen seventies, cartoons in journals mocked, warned and argued, from every side of politics.

slides.heading: Women and print

rows: Education at home, then girls' schools (from the mid-1800s)
Journals explaining why women should be educated
Rashsundari Debi, Amar Jiban (1876); Kailashbashini Debi (1860s)
Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai on upper-caste widows (1880s)
Fears that a literate girl would be widowed, or corrupted by romances
Battala books carried by pedlars into homes; journals by and for women in the early 1900s

visual.alt: Table of women and print: education at home and in girls' schools; women writers such as Rashsundari Debi and Kailashbashini Debi; Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai on widows; conservative opposition; and Battala books and women's journals

slides.narration: For many middle-class women, print opened a door. Liberal families taught daughters at home and later sent them to girls' schools. Women began to write: Rashsundari Debi, who learnt to read in secret in her kitchen, wrote the first full autobiography in Bengali. In Maharashtra, Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai wrote angrily about the lives of widows. Not everyone approved; some families feared what reading would do to girls.

slides.heading: Quick check: women readers
slides.body_md: Decide whether the assertion and the reason are true, and whether the reason explains the assertion.
slides.narration: Check each statement, then ask whether the fears explain the opposition.

slides.heading: Print and the poor; print against caste

rows: Gulamgiri (1871), on the injustices of caste
B.R. Ambedkar (Maharashtra) and E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker, Periyar (Madras)
Powerful writings on caste, read across India
Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal (1938), linking caste and class exploitation
Set up libraries, following Bombay workers

visual.alt: Table of print against caste and by workers: Phule's Gulamgiri of 1871; writings of Ambedkar and Periyar; Kashibaba's 1938 book; poems by a Kanpur millworker writing as Sudarshan Chakr; and libraries set up by Bangalore millworkers in the 1930s

slides.narration: Print also reached the poor. Cheap books were sold at crossroads, and public libraries spread from the early nineteen hundreds. People who had been pushed to the margins used print to speak. Jyotiba Phule wrote Gulamgiri against caste injustice. Ambedkar and Periyar wrote powerfully on caste. A Kanpur millworker named Kashibaba showed how caste and class oppression were linked. Workers in Bangalore set up their own libraries.

slides.heading: Print and censorship

nodes.label: 1820s: Calcutta Supreme Court regulations; pro-British papers encouraged
1835: Bentinck revises press laws; Macaulay restores earlier freedoms
After 1857: demands to clamp down on the "native" press
1878: Vernacular Press Act (modelled on the Irish Press Laws)
Warning, then seizure of press and machinery
Yet nationalist papers multiply; 1908: Tilak jailed, protests across India

visual.alt: Flow of press policy: regulations in the 1820s; Bentinck and Macaulay restore freedoms in 1835; demands for a clamp-down after 1857; the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 modelled on the Irish Press Laws, with warnings and seizure of presses; yet nationalist papers multiplied and Tilak's jailing in 1908 caused protests across India

slides.narration: Colonial policy on the press swung back and forth. In the eighteen twenties, courts brought in controls. In eighteen thirty-five, after petitions from editors, Bentinck and Macaulay restored freedoms. After eighteen fifty-seven, the mood hardened. The Vernacular Press Act of eighteen seventy-eight let officials warn papers and then seize their presses. Yet nationalist papers kept multiplying, and when Tilak was jailed in nineteen-oh-eight, protests erupted.

slides.heading: Quick check: 1878
slides.narration: A year is all you need. Think of the Act that targeted Indian-language newspapers.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a 5-mark "explain" answer
slides.body_md: Question: *"Print gave new voices to groups who had been unheard." Explain with five points from India.* (about 120 words)
bullets: Step 1 — One opening line: print let women, low castes and workers speak for themselves.
Step 2 — Plan five distinct groups or people: Rashsundari Debi; Tarabai Shinde or Pandita Ramabai; Phule; Ambedkar and Periyar; Kashibaba.
Step 3 — For each, name the work or theme in a few words.
Step 4 — Do not spend two points on the same person.

visual.alt: Table of five points: Rashsundari Debi and Amar Jiban; Tarabai Shinde or Pandita Ramabai on widows; Jyotiba Phule's Gulamgiri; Ambedkar and Periyar on caste; and Kashibaba on caste and class

slides.narration: This kind of question rewards specific names. Plan five voices, each with a work or theme: Rashsundari Debi's autobiography, writers on widows, Phule's Gulamgiri, Ambedkar and Periyar on caste, and a millworker, Kashibaba. One voice per point, one key term each. Vague answers like "women started writing" earn little. Precise names and works earn full marks.

slides.body_md: Arrange these events from earliest to latest.
slides.narration: Put a year beside each event first.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Palm leaf and paper; costly, fragile; Bengal schools taught writing by dictation
Sambad Kaumudi vs Samachar Chandrika; Deoband fatwas; Ramcharitmanas (1810); Naval Kishore Press
Novels, essays, Ravi Varma's prints, cartoons
Women writers; Phule, Ambedkar, Periyar; millworkers

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: manuscripts, the arrival of print, religion and print, new forms, new voices, and censorship

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. India moved from precious manuscripts to cheap print, starting with missionaries in Goa. Print turned religious argument into public debate. It gave India novels, essays, popular pictures and cartoons. It let women, low-caste writers and workers speak for themselves. And it alarmed the colonial state, which tried censorship, especially after eighteen fifty-seven, but could not stop the growth of a nationalist press.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: First press: **Goa**, Portuguese missionaries. Not Calcutta.
Sambad Kaumudi = Rammohun Roy (reform); Samachar Chandrika = orthodox reply.
Vernacular Press Act **1878**: warning first, then seizure of press.
Match writers to works: Phule–Gulamgiri; Rashsundari Debi–Amar Jiban; Tilak–Kesari.
For "print and censorship", show that repression did not stop the press.
slides.narration: Here are the traps for Part 2. The first press in India was in Goa, not Calcutta. Keep reformers and their opponents straight. Remember the two-step procedure of the Press Act: a warning, then seizure. Learn writers with their works, because matching questions are common. And in any answer on censorship, show both sides: the controls, and the growth of the press in spite of them.

notes.title: Print Culture and the Modern World — Notes

sections.heading: 1. The first printed books: East Asia and Europe
sections.body_md:
**China.** From **AD 594**, each page was carved into a **wooden block**, inked, and paper was pressed on it by hand. The soft, thin paper soaked up ink, so only one side could be used, so pages were folded into **accordion books** and stitched at the side. For centuries the **imperial state** was the chief printer, producing textbooks for the **civil service examinations**. By the **seventeenth century**, with a growing urban culture, **merchants** used print in trade, reading became a **leisure** activity (fiction, poetry, romantic plays), and **rich women** read and some published. In the **late nineteenth century** Western mechanical presses arrived and **Shanghai** emerged as the centre of the new printing trade.

**Japan.** Buddhist missionaries from China brought hand-printing around **AD 768–770**. The oldest Japanese printed book is the Buddhist **Diamond Sutra (AD 868)**, with six sheets of text and woodcut pictures. Books were cheap and plentiful in medieval Japan. In late eighteenth-century **Edo (Tokyo)**, **Kitagawa Utamaro** (born 1753) and others made **ukiyo** prints of city life.

**Europe.** **Marco Polo** brought knowledge of woodblock printing from China to Italy in **1295**. Woodblocks spread (textiles, playing cards, religious pictures), but books were mainly copied by **scribes**: slow, costly and fragile. Aristocrats long preferred luxury handwritten editions on **vellum**. **Johann Gutenberg** adapted the **olive press** and used moulds to cast **metal type**; by **1448** his system was perfected, and his first book was the **Bible** (about 180 copies, about three years). Between **1450 and 1550** presses spread across most of Europe; output grew from about **20 million** copies (late 1400s) to about **200 million** (1500s).

key_terms.definition_md: Printing by carving a whole page into a block of wood, inking it and pressing paper on it.
Separate metal letters that can be arranged, inked and reused to print any text.
A fine parchment made from animal skin, used for luxury manuscripts.
"Pictures of the floating world": Japanese prints of everyday urban life.

sections.heading: 2. The print revolution and its impact
sections.body_md:
- **Cheaper, faster books.** Mechanical printing cut the time, labour and cost of making books, which reached a much larger public.
- **A reading public.** Knowledge that was once **heard** could now be **read**. But literacy stayed low for a long time, so printers produced **ballads and folk tales**, often illustrated, that were **read aloud** at gatherings: oral and print culture mixed.
- **Fear of print.** Some feared that uncontrolled reading would spread **rebellious and irreligious** ideas. The scholar **Erasmus** worried that worthless books would bury real learning.
- **Luther and the Reformation.** In **1517** **Martin Luther** wrote the **Ninety Five Theses** against practices of the Roman Catholic Church. Printed copies spread at speed; his German **New Testament** sold out within weeks. Print helped the **Protestant Reformation**.
- **Dissent and control.** The miller **Menocchio** read books and formed his own ideas of God and Creation; the Church tried him twice and executed him. The Church controlled publishers and booksellers and kept an **Index of Prohibited Books** from **1558**.
- **The French Revolution.** Historians give three arguments: print spread **Enlightenment** ideas (Voltaire, Rousseau) attacking tradition, superstition and despotism; it built a new habit of **public argument**; and by the **1780s** it carried writing and cartoons **mocking royalty**. **Caution:** readers also read royal and Church writing and made up their own minds; print made new thinking possible but did not by itself cause the Revolution.

key_terms.definition_md: A large body of people who get knowledge and ideas by reading printed matter.
The sixteenth-century movement, begun by Luther, that broke with the Roman Catholic Church.
A Roman Catholic institution that identified and punished those whose beliefs it considered heretical.

visual.alt: Flow: cheap printed books created a reading public, which fed both the Reformation and dissent, leading to Church controls, and the Enlightenment debate before 1789

sections.heading: 3. The reading mania of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries
sections.body_md:
- **Literacy** rose as churches set up village schools; in some parts of Europe it reached **60–80 per cent** by the end of the eighteenth century.
- **Pedlars** sold almanacs, ballads and folk tales: **penny chapbooks** (England, carried by chapmen) and the **Biliotheque Bleue** (France, cheap books in blue covers).
- The **periodical press** mixed current affairs with entertainment; the ideas of **Isaac Newton**, **Thomas Paine**, **Voltaire** and **Rousseau** reached ordinary readers.
- **Children:** compulsory primary schooling meant textbooks; a **children's press** was set up in France in **1857**; the **Grimm brothers** published folk tales in **1812**, leaving out what seemed unfit for children or vulgar to the elite.
- **Women:** penny magazines and conduct manuals; women as readers and writers of novels — **Jane Austen**, the **Brontë sisters**, **George Eliot** — whose heroines made their own choices.
- **Workers:** **lending libraries** educated artisans and clerks; as working hours fell, workers wrote **political tracts and autobiographies**.
- **Technology:** metal presses by the late 1700s; **Richard M. Hoe's** power-driven cylindrical press (about **8,000 sheets an hour**), suited to newspapers; the **offset press** (up to six colours); electric presses, better paper feeding and plates.
- **New selling methods:** novels **serialised** in periodicals; cheap **shilling series** (1920s England); the **dust jacket**; **paperbacks** in the Depression of the 1930s.

key_terms.definition_md: A cheap pocket-sized book sold by pedlars (chapmen) in England.
Cheap French books on poor paper with blue covers.
A library that lends books for a small fee or free.

sections.heading: 4. India and the world of print (1): from manuscripts to newspapers
sections.body_md:
**Manuscripts.** India had an old tradition of handwritten books in **Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian** and many vernaculars, on **palm leaves** or **handmade paper**, often illustrated. They were **costly, fragile** and written in varied scripts, so were little used in daily life. In pre-colonial **Bengal**, village schools taught pupils to **write** from the teacher's dictation; pupils could write well yet had never handled a book.

**Arrival of print.** The first press came with **Portuguese missionaries to Goa** in the mid-sixteenth century; Jesuits learnt **Konkani** and printed tracts (about 50 books in Konkani and Kanara languages by 1674). Catholic priests printed the first **Tamil** book at **Cochin (1579)** and the first **Malayalam** book (**1713**); by 1710 Dutch Protestant missionaries had printed 32 Tamil texts.

**Newspapers.** From **1780**, **James Augustus Hickey** edited the weekly **Bengal Gazette**, which printed advertisements and gossip about senior Company officials; **Warren Hastings** persecuted him and encouraged officially approved papers. In **1816**, **Gangadhar Bhattacharya**, close to Rammohun Roy, brought out a weekly *Bengal Gazette*, the first Indian-run paper.

**Religious reform and debate.** Print widened argument about religion and custom. **Rammohun Roy** published **Sambad Kaumudi** from **1821**; orthodox Hindus answered with **Samachar Chandrika**. In **1822** came two Persian papers, **Jam-i-Jahan Nama** and **Shamsul Akhbar**, and the Gujarati **Bombay Samachar**. In north India the **ulama**, anxious about colonial rule and Muslim personal law, used cheap **lithographic** presses for Persian and Urdu translations and religious papers; the **Deoband Seminary (1867)** published thousands of **fatwas**. Among Hindus, the **Ramcharitmanas** of Tulsidas was first printed in Calcutta in **1810**; from the 1880s the **Naval Kishore Press** (Lucknow) and **Shri Venkateshwar Press** (Bombay) published religious texts in vernaculars, which were read aloud to the unlettered. Newspapers carried news across regions, helping create **pan-Indian identities**.

key_terms.definition_md: A cheap printing method using a flat stone or plate, widely used for Indian-language texts.
A legal opinion on Islamic law, given by a scholar.
The everyday language of a region, as opposed to a classical or foreign language.

visual.alt: Timeline table of print in India: the first press in Goa, the first Tamil book in 1579, Hickey's Bengal Gazette in 1780, the Ramcharitmanas printed in 1810, Sambad Kaumudi in 1821, and the Deoband Seminary in 1867

sections.heading: 5. India and the world of print (2): new forms, new readers, censorship
sections.body_md:
**New forms.** The **novel** took Indian forms; lyrics, short stories and essays on social and political themes appeared. **Raja Ravi Varma** produced images for mass circulation; wood engravers set up near presses; **cheap prints and calendars** spread. By the **1870s**, **cartoons** in journals commented on society and politics: some mocked Indians' taste for Western ways, some feared social change, some lampooned nationalists and some attacked imperial rule.

**Women.** Liberal families educated women at home and, from the mid-nineteenth century, sent them to **girls' schools**; journals argued for women's education. Some conservatives believed a literate girl would be **widowed**; some feared girls would be corrupted by **romances**. **Rashsundari Debi** learnt to read secretly in her kitchen and wrote **Amar Jiban (1876)**, the first full-length autobiography published in Bengali; **Kailashbashini Debi** wrote in the 1860s; **Tarabai Shinde** and **Pandita Ramabai** (1880s, Maharashtra) wrote with anger about upper-caste widows. **Ram Chaddha's** *Istri Dharm Vichar* taught obedience to wives. **Battala** in central Calcutta printed cheap religious and popular books, carried to homes by pedlars.

**The poor and caste.** Cheap small books were sold at crossroads in Madras towns; **public libraries** spread from the early twentieth century. **Jyotiba Phule** wrote **Gulamgiri (1871)** on caste injustice; **B.R. Ambedkar** and **E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker (Periyar)** wrote powerfully on caste. The Kanpur millworker **Kashibaba** wrote **Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal (1938)**, linking caste and class exploitation; another, writing as **Sudarshan Chakr**, wrote poems (1935–55) collected as *Sacchi Kavitayan*. **Bangalore** millworkers set up libraries in the 1930s, following Bombay workers.

**Censorship.** Before 1798 the Company was not much concerned; early controls targeted Englishmen critical of Company rule. In the **1820s** the Calcutta Supreme Court passed press regulations. In **1835**, after petitions, **Bentinck** agreed to revise press laws and **Macaulay** drafted rules restoring earlier freedoms. After **1857**, attitudes hardened. The **Vernacular Press Act (1878)**, modelled on the **Irish Press Laws**, allowed extensive censorship: papers were tracked; a report judged seditious drew a **warning**, and a paper that ignored it risked losing its **press and machines**. Nationalist papers nonetheless **multiplied**. When **Tilak** wrote sympathetically about deported Punjab revolutionaries in **Kesari** (1907), he was imprisoned in **1908**, provoking protests across India.

key_terms.definition_md: Official control over what may be printed or published.
Speech or writing that encourages rebellion against the state.
A law allowing the colonial government to censor Indian-language newspapers.

questions.stem_md: From about AD 594, books in China were printed by

options.text_md: casting metal letters in moulds and pressing them with a screw press
carving each page into a block of wood, inking it and pressing paper on it by hand
copying every page by hand on palm leaves
using power-driven cylinders

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Early Chinese printing was done by hand: a block of wood was carved, inked, and paper was rubbed against it.
Step 2: So (b).
Step 3: (a) describes Gutenberg's press of the fifteenth century; (c) is the manuscript tradition; (d) is a nineteenth-century invention.

questions.stem_md: Why was the traditional Chinese "accordion book" folded and stitched at the side?

options.text_md: Because the soft, thin paper soaked up ink, so only one side of each sheet could carry print
Because emperors banned bound books
Because it was cheaper to make than a scroll
Because metal type could not print on folded paper

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The paper used for block printing was soft and thin; ink came through to the back, so only one face of a sheet was usable.
Step 2: The printed sheets were therefore folded, with the blank sides inside, and stitched at the side: (a).

questions.stem_md: For a long time, the biggest producer of printed material in China was the imperial state. Why did it print so much?

options.text_md: To sell novels to merchants
To publish newspapers for factory workers
To supply textbooks for candidates preparing for the civil service examinations
To print the Bible for missionaries

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: China recruited officials through civil service examinations, and huge numbers of candidates needed the same texts.
Step 2: So the state printed textbooks in vast numbers: (c).
Step 3: Novels for merchants came later, in the seventeenth century; newspapers for workers and Bibles for missionaries are not part of this story.

questions.stem_md: The oldest Japanese printed book, from AD 868, is

options.text_md: the Gutenberg Bible
the Buddhist Diamond Sutra
a collection of ukiyo pictures
the Ninety Five Theses

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Buddhist missionaries from China brought hand-printing to Japan around AD 768–770.
Step 2: The oldest surviving Japanese book, printed in AD 868, is the Buddhist **Diamond Sutra**, with six sheets of text and woodcut pictures: (b).

questions.stem_md: How did knowledge of woodblock printing reach Italy?

options.text_md: Marco Polo brought it back from China in 1295.
Gutenberg learnt it in Japan.
Portuguese missionaries brought it from Goa.
Luther brought it from Wittenberg.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The explorer Marco Polo returned to Italy in 1295 after many years in China, bringing knowledge of woodblock printing.
Step 2: Italians began printing with woodblocks and the technology spread. So (a).
Step 3: The other options reverse the direction or mix up people and places.

questions.stem_md: Even after woodblock printing reached Europe, handwritten manuscripts could not meet the growing demand for books. Which statement best explains why?

options.text_md: Paper had not yet been invented in Europe.
Scribes refused to copy religious books.
Manuscripts were banned by the Church.
Copying by hand was slow, costly and laborious, and manuscripts were fragile.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Booksellers employed many scribes, yet copying by hand stayed slow and expensive, and manuscripts were fragile and awkward to handle.
Step 2: So production could not keep pace with demand: (d).
Step 3: (b) and (c) are false; (a) is wrong, paper was in use.

questions.stem_md: Johann Gutenberg grew up on a farm estate where he saw wine and olive presses, and later trained as a goldsmith who made lead moulds. How did these experiences help him?

options.text_md: He used them to make woodblocks more quickly.
He adapted the olive press into a printing press and used moulds to cast metal type for letters.
He used them to improve paper-making.
He used them to design the first steam press.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The screw press for olives gave him the model for a printing press.
Step 2: His skill with moulds let him cast movable **metal type** for each letter.
Step 3: So (b). Steam and power-driven presses came much later.

questions.stem_md: Which change best describes what printing did to the way people received knowledge in Europe?

options.text_md: It ended oral culture completely.
It made books more expensive, so only nobles read.
It created a reading public, while popular tales and songs were also printed and read aloud to those who could not read.
It made the Church the only source of books.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Cheaper, more plentiful books created a large **reading public**.
Step 2: But literacy stayed low for a long time, so printers produced ballads and folk tales that were read aloud in villages and taverns; oral and print culture overlapped.
Step 3: So (c). (a) and (b) are false, and (d) is the opposite: print weakened Church control over texts.

questions.stem_md: Erasmus, a Latin scholar and Catholic reformer, was uneasy about printing because he feared that

options.text_md: it would put scribes out of work
it would end the use of Latin completely
it would make the Bible too expensive
books full of foolish, scandalous or irreligious matter would flood the market and drown out valuable learning

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Erasmus worried that printers would fill the world with worthless and harmful books, and that serious learning would be lost among them.
Step 2: So (d). His concern was about the content and its effects, not about jobs or prices.

questions.stem_md: In 1517 Martin Luther wrote the Ninety Five Theses. What did they do, and how did print matter?

options.text_md: They praised the Pope; print spread them to the nobles only.
They criticised many practices and rituals of the Roman Catholic Church; printed copies spread his ideas widely and quickly.
They banned printing in Germany.
They were a list of prohibited books.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Luther's theses attacked practices and rituals of the Roman Catholic Church.
Step 2: His writings were printed in huge numbers and read widely, helping to start the **Protestant Reformation**. So (b).
Step 3: (d) describes the Church's Index, the opposite reaction.

questions.stem_md: Menocchio, a sixteenth-century miller in Italy, was punished by the Roman Catholic Church because he

options.text_md: ran an illegal printing press
refused to pay taxes to the Pope
read books and formed his own views of God and Creation, which the Church considered heretical
translated the Bible into German

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Menocchio read books available in his locality and reinterpreted the Bible's message in his own way.
Step 2: The Church, which was hunting down heretical ideas through its Inquisition, tried him twice and finally executed him. So (c).

questions.stem_md: From 1558 the Roman Church maintained a list called the Index of Prohibited Books. This is best seen as

options.text_md: an attempt to control what people could read, in response to the spread of printed ideas it considered dangerous
a catalogue of books printed by Gutenberg
a list of books given free to schools
a guide to buying cheap chapbooks

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Troubled by readers questioning its teachings, the Church imposed controls on publishers and booksellers.
Step 2: The Index listed books that Catholics were forbidden to read: an act of **censorship**, so (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following was **not** one of the arguments historians make about how print helped create the conditions for the French Revolution?

options.text_md: Print spread the ideas of Enlightenment thinkers such as Voltaire and Rousseau.
Print built a new habit of public argument in which old values were open to question.
By the 1780s, satire in print attacked the royal family's luxury and morals.
Print forced every French person to accept revolutionary ideas without question.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Options (a), (b) and (c) are the three main arguments.
Step 2: (d) is not an argument historians make: people also read royalist and Church writing and did not accept everything they read. Print opened the way to new thinking; it did not control minds. So (d).

questions.stem_md: An imagined cartoon sold in Paris in 1787 shows nobles feasting at a table while peasants carry them on their backs. What effect would such prints most likely have had?

options.text_md: They would make readers feel grateful to the nobility.
They would encourage readers to question a system in which the privileged lived off the poor.
They would teach readers how to print cartoons.
They would stop people from reading newspapers.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: By the 1780s, prints and pamphlets made fun of the royal family and nobles and set their luxury against the people's suffering.
Step 2: Such images encouraged readers to question the social order, so (b).

questions.stem_md: Pocket-sized books sold for a penny by travelling pedlars called chapmen in England were known as

options.text_md: chapbooks
Biliotheque Bleue
almanacs of the court
shilling novels

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: In England, **penny chapbooks** were carried by chapmen and sold so that even the poor could buy them.
Step 2: So (a). The Biliotheque Bleue were the French equivalent, cheap books with blue covers.

questions.stem_md: An imagined French village pedlar of the eighteenth century carries cheap little books printed on poor paper and bound in blue covers. These belonged to the

options.text_md: Index of Prohibited Books
Biliotheque Bleue
Shilling Series
Penny magazines for women

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Low-priced French books on poor-quality paper bound in cheap blue covers were called the **Biliotheque Bleue**.
Step 2: So (b).

questions.stem_md: By the end of the eighteenth century, literacy rates in some parts of Europe were as high as

options.text_md: 5 to 10 per cent
20 to 30 per cent
60 to 80 per cent
100 per cent

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: With churches setting up village schools and print spreading, literacy rose through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
Step 2: In some parts of Europe it reached 60 to 80 per cent by the end of the eighteenth century: (c).

questions.stem_md: The Grimm brothers spent years collecting folk tales from peasants and published them in 1812. What did they do before publishing?

options.text_md: They translated the tales into Latin.
They printed them as penny chapbooks only for adults.
They added stories about the French Revolution.
They left out anything considered unsuitable for children or vulgar to the elite.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Folk tales were changed as they entered print: the Grimms edited what they collected.
Step 2: Material judged unfit for children or crude in the eyes of the elite was dropped, so (d). This shows print shaping what children read.

questions.stem_md: Which group of novelists are among the best-known women writers of nineteenth-century Europe?

options.text_md: Jane Austen, the Brontë sisters and George Eliot
Voltaire, Rousseau and Thomas Paine
Erasmus, Luther and Menocchio
Tarabai Shinde, Pandita Ramabai and Rashsundari Debi

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Jane Austen, the Brontë sisters and George Eliot were leading women novelists; their heroines made their own choices in life.
Step 2: So (a).
Step 3: (b) and (c) are men of the Enlightenment and Reformation; (d) are Indian women writers of the nineteenth century.

questions.stem_md: By the mid-nineteenth century Richard M. Hoe of New York had perfected a power-driven cylindrical press. Which kind of publication gained most from it?

options.text_md: Newspapers
Handwritten manuscripts
Palm-leaf books
Woodblock scrolls

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Hoe's press could print about 8,000 sheets an hour.
Step 2: Such speed was most useful for **newspapers**, which had to be printed in large numbers every day: (a).

questions.stem_md: During the Great Depression of the 1930s, publishers in the West feared that sales would fall. How did they respond?

options.text_md: They stopped printing novels.
They returned to handwritten books.
They brought out cheap paperback editions.
They printed only for the rich.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: With buyers short of money, publishers needed cheaper books.
Step 2: They issued cheap **paperback** editions to keep sales going, so (c).

questions.stem_md: Before print came to India, manuscripts were not widely used in everyday life. Which reason is correct?

options.text_md: They were expensive and fragile, and written in scripts that were hard to read.
They were written only in English.
The British had banned them.
They were printed on cheap paper that tore easily.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Manuscripts on palm leaves or handmade paper were costly and fragile, had to be handled with care, and were written in different styles that were not easy to read.
Step 2: So (a). (b) and (c) are false; (d) confuses manuscripts with printed books.

questions.stem_md: The first printing press in India came with Portuguese missionaries to

options.text_md: Calcutta
Bombay
Goa
Madras

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Portuguese missionaries brought the first press to **Goa** in the mid-sixteenth century.
Step 2: Jesuit priests there learnt Konkani and printed tracts. So (c).

questions.stem_md: James Augustus Hickey's Bengal Gazette (from 1780) angered Governor-General Warren Hastings because it

options.text_md: was printed in Persian
published gossip about the Company's senior officials in India
supported the French
called for the end of British rule

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Hickey's weekly boasted of its independence, and it printed gossip about senior officials of the East India Company.
Step 2: Hastings persecuted Hickey and encouraged officially approved newspapers, so (b).

questions.stem_md: From 1821 Rammohun Roy published Sambad Kaumudi. How did orthodox Hindu groups respond?

options.text_md: They petitioned the British to close all presses.
They set up the Deoband Seminary.
They started the Bombay Samachar in Gujarati.
They commissioned the Samachar Chandrika to oppose his opinions.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Rammohun Roy used his paper to argue for social and religious reform.
Step 2: Orthodox Hindus answered through print: they commissioned the **Samachar Chandrika** to counter him. So (d).
Step 3: This shows print widening public debate: both sides used it.

questions.stem_md: The Deoband Seminary, founded in 1867, used print mainly to

options.text_md: print the Ramcharitmanas
print English novels
publish the Vernacular Press Act
publish a vast number of fatwas advising Muslims on everyday conduct and religious questions

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Anxious about colonial rule and possible changes to Muslim personal law, the ulama used cheap lithographic presses.
Step 2: Deoband published a very large number of **fatwas** explaining the meaning of Islamic doctrines and guiding everyday conduct: (d).

questions.stem_md: An imagined pilgrim in Benares in the 1880s buys a cheap, small printed copy of a sixteenth-century religious epic in Hindi and later reads it aloud to his neighbours. Which statement best describes what is happening?

options.text_md: Print was restricted to scholars and priests.
Cheap vernacular editions of religious texts were spreading, read by the faithful and read aloud to those who could not read.
The Vernacular Press Act had banned religious books.
Religious texts could only be bought in English.

questions.solution_md:

answer.model_answer_md: (i) In both, print let **critics of existing practice** spread ideas widely: **Luther** in Europe, **Rammohun Roy** in India. (ii) In both, **defenders** answered in print: the Church controlled books, and orthodox Hindus started the **Samachar Chandrika**. (iii) But Europe saw harsh **suppression** (the Index, Menocchio's execution), while in India rival groups mostly **argued in print**.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Similarity among critics.
Step 2: Similarity among defenders.
Step 3: A difference in how authority responded.

questions.stem_md: "Print freed Indian women in the nineteenth century." Do you agree? Give three points.

answer.model_answer_md: **Partly.** (i) Print gave some women **education and a voice**: Rashsundari Debi, Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai wrote about women's lives. (ii) But many families **opposed** women reading, and much print, like Istri Dharm Vichar, taught **obedience**. (iii) So print **opened doors** mainly for middle-class women; it did not free most women.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Evidence that print empowered women.
Step 2: Evidence of its limits.
Step 3: A balanced judgement.

questions.stem_md: Imagine you are a Bangalore cotton millworker in the 1930s who has helped set up a workers' library. Explain three reasons why the library matters, based on what such libraries actually did.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) It helps workers **educate themselves**, following the example of **Bombay** millworkers. (ii) Social reformers who support it hope to **reduce heavy drinking** and spread **literacy**. (iii) It spreads the message of **nationalism**, and lets workers read writers who, like **Kashibaba**, write about their lives.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Self-education.
Step 2: Reformers' aims.
Step 3: Nationalism and workers' writing.

questions.stem_md: "Print served those in power as well as those who challenged them." Evaluate this statement with examples from Europe and India.

answer.model_answer_md:
**I agree.**
1. **Challengers in Europe:** **Luther** spread his criticism of the Church through print, and **Enlightenment** writers attacked despotism before 1789.
2. **Power in Europe:** the Church used the **Inquisition** and the **Index of Prohibited Books**, and kings issued their own **decrees** and propaganda.
3. **Challengers in India:** reformers, women writers and **Phule, Ambedkar and Periyar** used print against custom and caste; nationalists built a growing press.
4. **Power in India:** the colonial state backed **approved papers** and passed the **Vernacular Press Act (1878)**.
5. **Judgement:** print served both, but because it was **cheap and hard to control**, it gave challengers more than rulers could take away.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Take a position.
Step 2: Give examples of both uses in each region.
Step 3: Weigh them and conclude.

questions.stem_md: Imagine you plan to start an Indian-language newspaper in Bombay in 1880. Using the history of print in India, explain five opportunities and risks you would face.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Readers:** a growing public, including women readers in middle-class homes, wants news and debate.
2. **Reaching non-readers:** papers are **read aloud**, so the audience is larger than the number of literate buyers.
3. **Cheap production:** **lithographic** and other cheap presses keep costs low.
4. **Risk of censorship:** under the **Vernacular Press Act (1878)**, a report judged seditious brings a **warning**, then the **press may be seized**.
5. **Opportunity in debate:** readers follow reform and religious arguments, as in **Sambad Kaumudi** and its rivals, and papers are linking regions, so a bold paper can gain influence despite the risk.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Identify opportunities from the growth of print.
Step 2: Identify the legal risk.
Step 3: Give a balanced plan.

questions.stem_md: Why did China's print culture shift from hand printing to mechanical printing in the late nineteenth century, with Shanghai as its centre?

options.text_md: The imperial state banned woodblocks.
Japanese missionaries brought metal type to Beijing.
The civil service examinations were moved to Shanghai.
Western powers set up outposts in China and brought mechanical presses, which served new Western-style schools.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: As Western powers established outposts in China, Western printing methods and mechanical presses arrived.
Step 2: Shanghai emerged as the centre of the new printing trade, supplying books to Western-style schools, so (d).
Step 3: The other options are invented.

questions.stem_md: An imagined news website publishes embarrassing gossip about senior government officials, and its owner soon faces official harassment while friendly outlets get support. Which episode from the history of print in India does this most resemble?

options.text_md: Rammohun Roy starting Sambad Kaumudi
Warren Hastings persecuting James Augustus Hickey and encouraging officially approved newspapers
Portuguese missionaries printing in Konkani
The Naval Kishore Press printing religious texts

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The pattern is gossip about officials, harassment of the publisher, and support for friendly papers.
Step 2: That is what happened when Hickey's Bengal Gazette wrote about Company officials and Hastings persecuted him while encouraging approved papers. So (b).
Step 3: The other options involve no conflict with officials.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Printing about 180 copies of Gutenberg's Bible took about three years.

**Reason (R):** Gutenberg had perfected his printing system by 1448.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true.
Step 2: R is true.
Step 3: R gives the date the system was ready; it does not explain why the Bible took three years (each page had to be set in type and printed, sheet by sheet). So (b).

questions.stem_md: Imagine you are the editor of an English-language newspaper in Calcutta writing to a friend in 1836. Give two reasons, based on real events, why you feel freer than you did ten years earlier.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) In the **1820s** the Calcutta Supreme Court had passed **regulations** to control the press. (ii) In **1835**, after petitions from editors, **Bentinck** agreed to revise the press laws, and **Macaulay** drafted rules that **restored** the earlier freedoms.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Recall the controls of the 1820s.
Step 2: Recall the changes of 1835.

questions.stem_md: Who did more to change Europe in the sixteenth century: Gutenberg, who made print possible, or Luther, who used it? Give your view with three points.

answer.model_answer_md: **Gutenberg**, in my view. (i) Without his **press and metal type**, books could not be produced cheaply and in **millions**. (ii) **Luther's** ideas spread so fast only because print already existed. (iii) Yet Luther showed print's **power to change belief**, so both mattered; Gutenberg laid the **foundation**.
